# 07 · Filesystem cleanup: old files, dry runs, log rotation

*Sample output: what the model solution actually produces, on the input shown.*

## The main problem: finding and cleaning old files

A log directory as it looks at 2026-09-17 10:00 UTC (sizes and ages are fixed so this
page is reproducible):

```text
app.log            250,000 bytes    60 days old
debug.log            2,000 bytes    45 days old
recent.log         300,000 bytes     2 days old
archive/old.log    150,000 bytes    90 days old
app.log.1            1,000 bytes     1 days old
app.log.2            1,000 bytes     2 days old
app.log.3            1,000 bytes     3 days old
app.log.4            1,000 bytes     4 days old
app.log.5            1,000 bytes     5 days old
```

`find_files(root, older_than_days=30, min_bytes=100_000)`:

```python
app.log
archive/old.log
```

Reading that: two of the nine. `debug.log` is old enough but too small to be worth
deleting, and `recent.log` is big but current. Both filters have to pass.

Now the cleanup, which uses its own defaults (every file, any size) — `dry_run=True`
is what you run at 3am before you trust it:

```python
cleanup(root, older_than_days=30, dry_run=True, now=NOW)
  files   -> ['app.log', 'archive/old.log', 'debug.log']
  bytes   -> 402,000
  deleted -> False
```

Nothing has gone yet:

```python
['app.log', 'app.log.1', 'app.log.2', 'app.log.3', 'app.log.4', 'app.log.5', 'archive/old.log', 'debug.log', 'recent.log']
```

The same call with `dry_run=False`:

```python
cleanup(root, older_than_days=30, dry_run=False, now=NOW)
  files   -> ['app.log', 'archive/old.log', 'debug.log']
  bytes   -> 402,000
  deleted -> True

what's left on disk:
['app.log.1', 'app.log.2', 'app.log.3', 'app.log.4', 'app.log.5', 'recent.log']
```

Reading that: identical report, one field different. The `deleted` flag is what keeps
the log line honest — "would delete 402,000 bytes" and "deleted 402,000 bytes" are very
different sentences, and the caller can tell which happened without guessing.

Rotation is the other half, by count rather than age — `rotate(root, 'app.log.*', keep=2)`:

```python
removed -> ['app.log.3', 'app.log.4', 'app.log.5']
left    -> ['app.log.1', 'app.log.2', 'recent.log']
```

Reading that: newest two kept, the rest gone, ordered by mtime and never by name —
sorting `app.log.10` by name would put it before `app.log.9` and rotate the wrong file.

## The variant: grandfather-father-son backup retention

Input, a backup bucket listing on 2026-09-17 (a Thursday). Keep the last 7 daily, the
last 4 Sunday and the last 6 first-of-month backups:

```text
db-2026-09-17.sql.gz
db-2026-09-16.sql.gz
db-2026-09-15.sql.gz
db-2026-09-14.sql.gz
db-2026-09-13.sql.gz
db-2026-09-12.sql.gz
db-2026-09-11.sql.gz
db-2026-09-10.sql.gz
db-2026-09-06.sql.gz
db-2026-09-01.sql.gz
db-2026-08-30.sql.gz
db-2026-08-23.sql.gz
db-2026-08-16.sql.gz
db-2026-08-01.sql.gz
db-2026-07-01.sql.gz
db-2026-07-15.sql.gz
db-2026-09-18.sql.gz
db-2026-02-30.sql.gz
db-2026-09-14.sql.gz.tmp
notes.txt
```

`backups_to_delete(filenames, today=date(2026, 9, 17), daily=7, weekly=4, monthly=6)`:

```python
delete  db-2026-07-15.sql.gz
delete  db-2026-08-16.sql.gz
delete  db-2026-09-10.sql.gz
```

Everything it left alone:

```python
keep    db-2026-02-30.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-07-01.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-08-01.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-08-23.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-08-30.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-01.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-06.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-11.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-12.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-13.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-14.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-14.sql.gz.tmp
keep    db-2026-09-15.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-16.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-17.sql.gz
keep    db-2026-09-18.sql.gz
keep    notes.txt
```

Reading that: 16 real backups, 3 deleted. Each survivor is claimed by at least one rule.
09-17 back to 09-11 are the last 7 daily. 09-13, 09-06, 08-30 and 08-23 are the last 4
Sundays. 09-01, 08-01 and 07-01 are first-of-month. The three that go are the ones no
rule wants: 09-10 has just dropped out of the daily window, 08-16 is the *fifth* Sunday
back, and 07-15 is an ordinary Wednesday in July.

Note what 'last 4 Sundays' means here: the 4 most recent Sunday backups that EXIST, not
the last 4 calendar weeks. If the backup job dies for a month, a calendar window would
quietly delete everything, which is precisely when you need the old copies.

The four files that aren't ours are never touched, and they're the real safety story:
`notes.txt` and the `.tmp` partial upload don't match the pattern, `db-2026-02-30` has
the right shape but isn't a real date, and `db-2026-09-18` is dated tomorrow — clock
skew is not a reason to destroy a backup. Retention code should fail towards keeping
too much, never towards deleting something it didn't understand.
